summary: Arabic has no verb “to have”. It says “at me (is) …”: عِنْدِي كِتَابٌ = I have a book. The preposition عِنْدَ (“at, with”) takes the possessive suffixes — عِنْدِي, عِنْدَكَ, عِنْدَكِ, عِنْدَهُ, عِنْدَهَا, عِنْدَنَا, عِنْدَكُمْ, عِنْدَهُمْ — or a noun in the genitive: عِنْدَ أَبِي ثَلَاثَةُ إِخْوَةٍ (my father has three brothers). The thing you have is the grammatical subject: nominative, usually indefinite, after عِنْدَ…. Because عِنْدَ is not a verb, the past is made with كَانَ (كَانَ عِنْدِي, I had) and the negative with لَيْسَ (لَيْسَ عِنْدِي, lesson 8). Two more ways exist: لِي (“for me”, for relatives and lasting things: لِي أَخٌ) and مَعِي (“with me”, on you right now: مَعِي قَلَمٌ).

head: who has
عِنْدَ + suffix
example
rows: عِنْدِي أَخٌ. — I have a brother.
عِنْدَكَ أُخْتٌ؟ — Do you have a sister?
عِنْدَكِ أَطْفَالٌ؟ — Do you have children?
عِنْدَهُ زَوْجَةٌ. — He has a wife.
عِنْدَهَا رَضِيعٌ. — She has a baby.
عِنْدَنَا بَيْتٌ. — We have a house.
عِنْدَكُمْ أَوْلَادٌ؟ — Do you have children?
عِنْدَهُمْ أَرْبَعَةُ أَحْفَادٍ. — They have four grandchildren.
عِنْدَ أَبِي ثَلَاثَةُ إِخْوَةٍ. — My father has three brothers.

blocks.title: What you have is the subject.
blocks.text: In عِنْدِي أَخٌ the word أَخٌ is the subject of a sentence without a verb (“a brother is at me”): nominative -un, not accusative. Compare German Ich habe einen Bruder (accusative) — Arabic says عِنْدِي أَخٌ.

blocks.title: The past: add كَانَ.
blocks.text: كَانَ عِنْدِي بَيْتٌ (I had a house), كَانَ عِنْدَ جَدِّي بَيْتٌ (my grandfather had a house). Before a feminine thing both كَانَ and كَانَتْ are correct: كَانَ / كَانَتْ عِنْدِي سَيَّارَةٌ.

items.title: عِنْدِي
points: things you own or keep, family, time, a question

items.title: لِي
points: relatives and lasting relations: لِي أَخٌ, لِي أَصْدِقَاءُ كَثِيرُونَ

items.title: مَعِي
points: what you carry right now: مَعِي قَلَمٌ

blocks.text: Formal writing also uses لَدَى: لَدَيَّ (I have), لَدَيْكَ (you have) — the same idea, “at me”. Russian у меня есть and Turkish bende var build “to have” in exactly this way.

askYourself: Who has it? → choose the suffix on عِنْدَ: -ī, -ka / -ki, -hu / -hā, -nā, -kum, -hum.
Is the owner a noun? → عِنْدَ + the noun in the genitive (عِنْدَ أُخْتِي, عِنْدَ الْمُعَلِّمِ).
What is owned? → nominative, normally indefinite, after عِنْدَ…: عِنْدِي كِتَابٌ.
Was it in the past? → كَانَ before it: كَانَ عِنْدِي.
A relative or a lasting relation? → لِي also works; something on you right now? → مَعِي.

traps: Not accusative: عِنْدِي أَخٌ, not *عِنْدِي أَخًا.
عِنْدِي already contains “I”: أَنَا is not needed.
To a man عِنْدَكَ, to a woman عِنْدَكِ — unvocalized both are عندك.
عِنْدَ is a preposition, not a verb: it never takes verb endings; the tense comes from كَانَ.

quiz.why: عِنْدِي + the owned thing in the nominative.
The past comes from كَانَ; the house stays the subject (nominative).
عِنْدَ + the owner in the genitive; أَخ is masculine → ثَلَاثَةُ.

quiz.q: German haben, Greek έχω — what does Arabic use instead?
quiz.why: Arabic has no verb “to have”; it says “at me (is)”.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew has no “to have” either: יֵשׁ לִי (yesh li, “there is to me”) — with the preposition “to”, the twin of Arabic لِي.
German has a real verb, haben, with an accusative object (Ich habe einen Bruder); in Arabic the owned thing is a nominative subject.
Chinese has a verb, 有 (yǒu), negated with 没 (没有); it also means “there is”.
The endings of عِنْدِي, عِنْدَكَ … are the possessive endings of كِتَابِي, كِتَابُكَ …
